title: Stability Anchors and Load Sequencing Manifest
content:
Purpose:
This document captures a practical, reproducible manifest for throughput benchmarking runs that focuses on: stability anchors (deterministic signals we expect to hold across runs), load sequencing (how we schedule and prime traffic), and hygiene steps for repeatability. Its intentionally operational: copyable commands, config snippets, and a short checklist you can follow before a run.

Motivation / problem statement:
- We repeatedly see run-to-run variance driven by thermal drift, kernel scheduling, KV-cache state, and loadgen randomness.
- Teams need a lightweight, copy/pasteable procedure that reduces tail variance and surfaces real regressions, not noise.
- This is not a formal acceptance test; its an engineering harness for comparative throughput experiments.

Key terms (how we use them here):
- Stability anchor: an observable metric or small step whose value should be invariant across experiments (e.g., single-request p95 on an idle instance, or a small priming sequence RTT).
- Priming/warmup: a sequence of requests sent prior to measuring that brings caches, kernels, and accelerator state to a steady operational point.
- Load sequencing: ordering of traffic phases (ramp, anchor probes, plateau, microbursts) planned to isolate effects.

Overall experiment template (high-level):
1) Environment reset and baseline capture (5-10m)
  - Node-level sanity (GPU temp, fan, clocks)
  - Capture idle latency anchor: 10 single-request probes at inter-arrival 2s
2) Controlled warmup (10-30m)
  - Stepwise increase in qps with prefix-seeded requests to populate KV cache
  - Include small constant-rate background traffic to simulate multi-tenant interference if required
3) Stability anchor probes (every 5 minutes)
  - 50 single-request probes at moderate concurrency (c=4) to ensure anchors stable
4) Measurement plateau (20m)
  - Target qps held using pacing shim; collect full telemetry
5) Microburst stress checks (3x short bursts)
  - 30s bursts at 2-3x plateau qps to exercise scheduler and batching heuristics
6) Cooldown observation (5m)
  - Ensure metrics return to baseline; capture final anchors and resource state

Load generator configuration examples (copyable):
- Minimal JSON profile snippet (used by our loadgen wrapper):

{
  "name": "plateau-anchors-1",
  "phases": [
    {"type": "idle-probe", "duration_s": 60, "arrival_distribution": "poisson", "rate": 0.5},
    {"type": "ramp", "duration_s": 600, "from_qps": 1, "to_qps": 200},
    {"type": "plateau", "duration_s": 1200, "qps": 200, "concurrency": 8},
    {"type": "microburst", "duration_s": 30, "qps": 600},
    {"type": "cooldown", "duration_s": 300, "qps": 0.5}
  ]
}

Notes on that profile: the "idle-probe" is the stability anchor probe. We use poisson arrivals for the ramp to reduce simultaneous burst artifacts.

Priming recipes (practical):
- Short model priming sequence (when KV cache matters): send 8 copies of the canonical prompt family used in production at c=2, spaced 100ms apart. Repeat the family 3x during ramp.
- Thermal priming: sustained 60% of target QPS for 10 minutes to allow GPU clocks to settle. If you see slow drift in latency after this period, increase thermal priming to 20 minutes.

Seed hygiene and RNG control:
- Ensure loadgen RNG seeds are fixed between comparative runs (we embed the seed in run metadata).
- When testing quantization or kernel changes, keep sample prompts identical and pinned to a sha’ed corpus. Store corpus in artifacts repo and reference the sha in run metadata.

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- Client-side: per-request latency percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99), QPS, retries, http error codes, response sizes
- Server-side: per-token execution time, request queue length, batch size distribution, batch formation latency, GPU util, GPU power draw, GPU temperature, CPU steal, NIC rx/tx, disk I/O (rarely relevant but capture), kernel preemption events if available
- Platform: autoscaler decisions, node churn events, network egress/policy rejections

Stability anchors (recommended set):
1) Idle single-request p95 (10 probes) 
2) Small-prefix KV probe latency (50 probes)
3) Batch formation median at low qps (where batching should be minimal)
4) GPU clock and temp recorded at baseline

Decision thresholds for a run being valid:
- Idle single-request p95 must be within ±3% of previous run baseline OR we mark run invalid for comparative claims.
- Batch size distribution at plateau must not shift by >1 in median unless intentionally testing batching changes.
- Thermal drift: if GPU temperature rises by >8C during plateau relative to baseline run, tag as "thermal-variant" and annotate separately.

Failure modes and investigation hints:
- Symptom: plateau p99 spikes after 10 minutes.
  - Check for kernel eviction events, OS background jobs (cron, apt), thermal throttling.
  - Inspect batch formation traces: are large batches forming unpredictably? That points to arrival pattern changes.
- Symptom: lower throughput than expected with high GPU idle.
  - Check model fanout, model loading times, KV cache miss rates. Also verify that request shapes match model input sizes used during profiling.
- Symptom: reproducible but small regression (~4-6%):
  - Verify RNG seeds, corpus sha, env vars that affect CUDA kernels (e.g., CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING), compiler flags, and microcode/driver versions.

Run metadata and naming convention (important for dataset slicing):
- Use this format: "run/<model>-<variant>/plateau-<qps>-seed-<seed>/date-<YYYYMMDD>-tag-<short>"
- Example: run/gpt-mini/v1/plateau-200-seed-8421/date-20250109-tag-primeshield
- Always attach: commit sha for runtime, docker image tag, driver/kernel versions, exact loadgen profile file, and corpus sha

Quick commands (helpers):
- Start a baseline probe: 
  ./loadgenctl run --profile profiles/idle_probe.json --metadata "seed=8421,sha=abcd1234"
- Capture server-side telemetry (one-liner for the agent):
  ssh node-01 'sudo dstat -cdn 5 240 > /tmp/dstat.log & nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,power.draw --format=csv -l 5 > /tmp/gpu.csv &'
- Aggregate artifacts:
  ./run-artifact-collector --run-dir /tmp/current-run --out s3://redwood-benchmarks/runs/$(date +%Y%m%d)-8421

Interpretation rubric (quick):
- If plateau p50 improves and p99 degrades -> likely variance/queuing differences or batching tail effects.
- If all percentiles shift uniformly -> likely deterministic perf change (kernel/quantization/compilation path).

Notes to self / unresolved questions (work in progress):
- We still need a compact automated test to assert "anchor stability" preconditionally before flagging run as valid. Prototype in PR 678 but not merged.
- Microburst phase duration and intensity need tuning per model family; current defaults are conservative.
- Consider adding a small network jitter emulator for runs that want to reproduce multi-region jitter.

Appendix: example minimal run manifest (YAML-ish plain text)

run_name: stability-anchor-20250109
runtime_sha: abcd1234
loadgen_profile: profiles/plateau-200.json
seed: 8421
plateau_qps: 200
plateau_duration_s: 1200
warmup_thermal_minutes: 10
corpus_sha: corpora/promptset/v1/sha:deadbeef
notes: "Baseline comparison vs 20250102 nominal run"

References and links:
- Related ticket: JIRA INFR-122 (benchmark instability investigations)
- Prototype harness PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/678
- Confluence: serving-runtime/benchmarking-notes (internal)

If you use this manifest: copy the profile, pin the artifacts, and paste the run name into the run tracker spreadsheet. If anchors fail, stop and investigate before claiming a regression.

-- aisha
